claim: Metazoans establish mutually beneficial interactions with their resident microorganisms.
source: Metazoans establish mutually beneficial interactions with their resident microorganisms (McFall-Ngai et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to McFall-Ngai et al., 2013

claim: Microbial interactions contribute to different aspects of host physiology, including juvenile growth.
source: These interactions contribute to different aspects of host physiology, including juvenile growth, a postnatal developmental process marked by rapid body-size increase and organ maturation (Schwarzer et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schwarzer et al., 2018

claim: Juvenile growth is a postnatal developmental process marked by rapid body-size increase and organ maturation.
source: These interactions contribute to different aspects of host physiology, including juvenile growth, a postnatal developmental process marked by rapid body-size increase and organ maturation (Schwarzer et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schwarzer et al., 2018

claim: Juvenile growth results from the integration of environmental cues with the organism's intrinsic genetic potential, driven by energy and nutritional demands.
source: Juvenile growth results from the integration of environmental cues with the organism's intrinsic genetic potential, driven by energy and nutritional demands.
evidence: Based on established scientific understanding of developmental biology

claim: Harsh environmental conditions, notably nutrient deprivation, result in linear and ponderal growth failure (i.e. stunting).
source: Harsh environmental conditions, notably nutrient deprivation, result in linear and ponderal growth failure (i.e. stunting) (Nabwera et al., 2022), as well as alteration in gut microbiota maturation (Subramanian et al., 2014), which can be mitigated by microbial interventions and/or microbiota-directed nutritional interventions (Barratt et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nabwera et al., 2022, Subramanian et al., 2014, and Barratt et al., 2022

claim: Nutrient deprivation results in alteration in gut microbiota maturation.
source: Harsh environmental conditions, notably nutrient deprivation, result in linear and ponderal growth failure (i.e. stunting) (Nabwera et al., 2022), as well as alteration in gut microbiota maturation (Subramanian et al., 2014), which can be mitigated by microbial interventions and/or microbiota-directed nutritional interventions (Barratt et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Subramanian et al., 2014

claim: Growth failure and microbiota alterations from undernutrition can be mitigated by microbial interventions and/or microbiota-directed nutritional interventions.
source: Harsh environmental conditions, notably nutrient deprivation, result in linear and ponderal growth failure (i.e. stunting) (Nabwera et al., 2022), as well as alteration in gut microbiota maturation (Subramanian et al., 2014), which can be mitigated by microbial interventions and/or microbiota-directed nutritional interventions (Barratt et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barratt et al., 2022

claim: The understanding of how gut microbes buffer the deleterious effect of undernutrition and contribute to healthy juvenile growth remains elusive.
source: Despite some recent advances, the understanding of how gut microbes buffer the deleterious effect of undernutrition and contribute to healthy juvenile growth remains elusive.
evidence: Authors' assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field

claim: Drosophila melanogaster is a valuable experimental model to study the physiological consequences and underlying mechanisms of host–commensal bacteria interactions.
source: Drosophila melanogaster (referred here as Drosophila) is a valuable experimental model to study the physiological consequences and underlying mechanisms of host–commensal bacteria interactions (Douglas, 2018; Grenier and Leulier, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Douglas, 2018 and Grenier and Leulier, 2020

claim: Bacterial strains associated with Drosophila influence multiple physiological processes, including juvenile growth.
source: Bacterial strains associated with Drosophila influence multiple physiological processes, including juvenile growth, and on several occasions, the underlying symbiotic cues, that is, bacterial molecules directly impacting host functionalities, have been identified.
evidence: Based on established research in the field

claim: Amino acids produced by symbiotic bacteria can inhibit the production of the neuropeptide CNMamide in the gut, which shapes food foraging behavior by repressing preference for amino acids.
source: For instance, amino acids produced by symbiotic bacteria can inhibit the production of the neuropeptide CNMamide in the gut, which shape food foraging behavior by repressing preference for amino acids (Kim et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2021

claim: Bacterial metabolite acetate produced by strains of Acetobacter pomorum is necessary to support juvenile growth.
source: Bacterial metabolite such as acetate produced by strains of Acetobacter pomorum is necessary to support juvenile growth (Shin et al., 2011) by altering the epigenome of enteroendocrine cells and stimulating the secretion of the intestinal hormone Tachykinin (Jugder et al., 2021; Kamareddine et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shin et al., 2011

claim: Acetate from Acetobacter pomorum supports juvenile growth by altering the epigenome of enteroendocrine cells and stimulating the secretion of the intestinal hormone Tachykinin.
source: Bacterial metabolite such as acetate produced by strains of Acetobacter pomorum is necessary to support juvenile growth (Shin et al., 2011) by altering the epigenome of enteroendocrine cells and stimulating the secretion of the intestinal hormone Tachykinin (Jugder et al., 2021; Kamareddine et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jugder et al., 2021 and Kamareddine et al., 2018

claim: Peptidoglycan fragments from Lactiplantibacillus plantatum cell walls are directly sensed by peptidoglycan recognition receptors (PGRPs) in Drosophila enterocytes.
source: In the context of microbe-mediated Drosophila juvenile growth promotion (Storelli et al., 2011), peptidoglycan (PG) fragments from Lactiplantibacillus plantatum (Lp) cell walls are directly sensed by peptidoglycan recognition receptors (PGRPs) in Drosophila enterocytes.
evidence: Based on established research cited in the manuscript

claim: PG recognition by PGRPs signals via the IMD/NF-kappaB pathway to promote the production of intestinal peptidases, which helps juveniles optimize the assimilation of dietary proteins to support their systemic growth.
source: This recognition signal, via the IMD/NF-kappaB pathway, promotes the production of intestinal peptidases, which helps juveniles optimizing the assimilation of dietary proteins to support their systemic growth (Erkosar et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Erkosar et al., 2015

claim: The pbpX2-dltXABCD operon was identified as an important determinant of Lp-induced Drosophila larval growth through forward genetic screening.
source: Recently, in an effort to further characterize the bacterial machinery involved in Lp-mediated juvenile growth promotion, we identified through forward genetic screening the pbpX2-dltXABCD operon as an important determinant of Lp-induced Drosophila larval growth (Matos et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matos et al., 2017

claim: The first gene of the pbpX2-dltXABCD operon, pbpX2 (renamed dltE), is annotated as a serine-type D-Ala-D-Ala-carboxypeptidase putatively involved in PG maturation cleaving the terminal D-alanine residue of the peptide stem in newly made muropeptides.
source: The first gene of the operon, pbpX2 (here renamed dltE for D-Ala-LTA Esterase, see below), is uncharacterized and annotated as a serine-type D-Ala-D-Ala-carboxypeptidase putatively involved in PG maturation cleaving the terminal D-alanine (D-Ala) residue of the peptide stem in newly made muropeptides.
evidence: Based on bioinformatic annotation

claim: Lp PG precursors do not contain a terminal D-Ala in peptide stems but a terminal D-lactate (D-Lac).
source: Remarkably, Lp PG precursors do not contain a terminal D-Ala in peptide stems but a terminal D-lactate (D-Lac) (Ferain et al., 1996) raising the question of the biochemical activity of DltE.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferain et al., 1996

claim: The dltABCD genes encode a multi-protein machinery responsible for the D-alanylation of teichoic acids (TA) in diverse Gram-positive bacteria and in Lp.
source: On the other hand, the remaining dltABCD encode a multi-protein machinery responsible for the D-alanylation of teichoic acids (TA) in diverse Gram-positive bacteria (Perego et al., 1995) and in Lp (Nikolopoulos et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Perego et al., 1995 and Nikolopoulos et al., 2022

claim: Teichoic acids are anionic polymers localized within the Gram-positive bacteria cell wall, representing up to 50% of the cell envelope dry weight.
source: TAs are anionic polymers localized within the Gram-positive bacteria cell wall, representing up to 50% of the cell envelope dry weight and present in two forms: wall teichoic acids (WTAs), which are covalently bound to PG, and lipoteichoic acids (LTAs), which are anchored to the cytoplasmic membrane (Rohde, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rohde, 2019

claim: Teichoic acids are present in two forms: wall teichoic acids (WTAs), which are covalently bound to PG, and lipoteichoic acids (LTAs), which are anchored to the cytoplasmic membrane.
source: TAs are anionic polymers localized within the Gram-positive bacteria cell wall, representing up to 50% of the cell envelope dry weight and present in two forms: wall teichoic acids (WTAs), which are covalently bound to PG, and lipoteichoic acids (LTAs), which are anchored to the cytoplasmic membrane (Rohde, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rohde, 2019

claim: The dlt operon is essential to D-Ala esterification to the cell envelope in LpNC8.
source: Study of an isogenic mutant of Lp NC8 (LpNC8) strain, deleted for the entire dlt operon, revealed that this operon is indeed essential to D-Ala esterification to the cell envelope (most likely on TAs) and that purified D-alanylated cell envelopes triggered intestinal peptidase expression and support Drosophila juvenile growth (Matos et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matos et al., 2017

claim: Purified D-alanylated cell envelopes from LpNC8 triggered intestinal peptidase expression and support Drosophila juvenile growth.
source: Study of an isogenic mutant of Lp NC8 (LpNC8) strain, deleted for the entire dlt operon, revealed that this operon is indeed essential to D-Ala esterification to the cell envelope (most likely on TAs) and that purified D-alanylated cell envelopes triggered intestinal peptidase expression and support Drosophila juvenile growth (Matos et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matos et al., 2017

claim: DltE is structurally homologous to the D-Ala-D-Ala carboxypeptidase R61 (DDCP) from Streptomyces.
source: DltE is structurally homologous to the D-Ala-D-Ala carboxypeptidase R61 (DDCP) from Streptomyces (Figure 1b and c; Kelly et al., 1986; McDonough et al., 2002) that exhibits the classical β-lactamase fold of PBPs (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1 and citations to Kelly et al., 1986 and McDonough et al., 2002

claim: The catalytic S-X-X-K motif (128SIQK131) is conserved in DltE.
source: The positions of the active site S-X-X-K motif (128SIQK131), containing the catalytic Ser128 and Lys131 residues, and the catalytic Tyr213 from the second motif are conserved (Figure 1a and b and Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by structural data shown in Figures 1 and 2

claim: The global architecture of the active site cavity of DltE is reshaped and different from that of DDCP enzymes, adopting a deeper cleft topology largely opened on both sides of the protein.
source: The global architecture of the active site cavity of DltE is therefore reshaped and different from that of DDCP enzymes, adopting a deeper cleft topology largely opened on both sides of the protein (Figure 1d–g).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 1d-g

claim: DltE's structural features strongly suggest that it possesses an alternative substrate recognition mode and/or a different substrate specificity than PBPs.
source: Together with its inability to bind penicillin, such structural features strongly suggest that DltE possesses an alternative substrate recognition mode and/or a different substrate specificity than PBPs.
evidence: Based on inference from structural and biochemical data

claim: DltE is not able to cleave the ester bond between D-Ala4 and D-Lac5 from the disaccharide-depsipentapeptide.
source: We observed that DltE was not able to cleave the ester bond between D-Ala4 and D-Lac5 from the disaccharide-depsipentapeptide, whereas purified DacA1 efficiently did (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: DacA1 efficiently cleaves the ester bond between D-Ala4 and D-Lac5 from the disaccharide-depsipentapeptide.
source: We observed that DltE was not able to cleave the ester bond between D-Ala4 and D-Lac5 from the disaccharide-depsipentapeptide, whereas purified DacA1 efficiently did (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3

claim: DltE is not a carboxylesterase active on PG stem depsipentapeptide.
source: These results indicate that DltE is not a carboxylesterase active on PG stem depsipentapeptide.
evidence: Based on experimental results showing lack of activity on PG substrate

claim: LTA from LpNC8 is constituted by repetitive units of glycerol (Gro)-phosphate chains that were either unsubstituted (Unit A) or substituted with either Ala (Unit B), α-Glc (Unit C) or Ala-6-αGlc (Unit D) groups at C-2 position of Gro residues.
source: In contrast to WTA, NMR analysis established that LTA from LpNC8 is constituted by repetitive units of glycerol (Gro)-phosphate chains that were either unsubstituted (Unit A) or substituted with either Ala (Unit B), α-Glc (Unit C) or Ala-6-αGlc (Unit D) groups at C-2 position of Gro residues (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by NMR analysis shown in Figure 3b

claim: WTA from LpNC8 contained two main repetition units composed of ribitol (Rbo)-phosphate chains substituted by two α-Glc residues either in C-2 and C-4 positions (major unit) or in C-3 and C-4 positions (minor unit).
source: Multidimensional NMR spectroscopy analysis revealed that WTA from LpNC8 contained two main repetition units composed of ribitol (Rbo)-phosphate chains substituted by two α-Glc residues either in C-2 and C-4 positions (major unit) or in C-3 and C-4 positions (minor unit) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: Supported by NMR analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2b

claim: No Ala substituents were detected in WTA from LpNC8.
source: Remarkably, no Ala substituents were detected.
evidence: Based on NMR analysis of WTA

claim: WTAs purified from ΔdltXABCD were structurally identical from those purified from LpNC8.
source: WTAs purified from ΔdltXABCD were structurally identical from those purified from LpNC8, which supports that the DltXABCD complex is not involved in the D-alanylation of WTA.
evidence: Based on NMR comparison of WTA from different strains

claim: The DltXABCD complex is not involved in the D-alanylation of WTA.
source: WTAs purified from ΔdltXABCD were structurally identical from those purified from LpNC8, which supports that the DltXABCD complex is not involved in the D-alanylation of WTA.
evidence: Based on inference from structural identity of WTA in WT and mutant strains

claim: NMR analysis of LTA extracted from ΔdltXABCD mutant confirmed the absence of Ala-substituted LTA.
source: NMR analysis of LTA extracted from ΔdltXABCD mutant confirmed the absence of Ala-substituted LTA, as demonstrated by the disappearance of GroB-2 and GroB1,3 signals, GlcD-6 signals and Ala-2 signals on the 1H-13C HSQC spectrum and of GroB1 to 3 signals on the 1H-1H COSY spectrum (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by NMR analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Only LTAs are D-alanylated in LpNC8 cell envelope.
source: Taken together, these results establish that LpNC8 cell envelope carries LTAs with a distinctive pattern of structure and substitution and that only LTAs are D-alanylated.
evidence: Based on NMR analysis of both WTA and LTA

claim: The Dlt machinery is necessary to the D-alanylation of Lp LTAs.
source: In addition, these observations confirm that the Dlt machinery is necessary to the D-alanylation of Lp LTAs.
evidence: Based on comparison of LTA from WT and ΔdltXABCD mutant

claim: DltEextra was able to efficiently bind LTA.
source: As shown in Figure 3c, DltEextra was able to efficiently bind LTA.
evidence: Supported by MST data shown in Figure 3c

claim: Upon incubation of LTA with DltE, there was a clear decrease (56% decrease) of Gro-Ala and a concomitant increase of free D-Ala.
source: Upon incubation of LTA with DltE, we observed a clear decrease (56% decrease) of Gro-Ala and a concomitant increase of free D-Ala.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS analysis of enzymatic reaction products

claim: The effect of DltE on Gro-Ala was enhanced (64% decrease) with a double amount of DltEextra in the test.
source: This effect was enhanced (64% decrease) with a double amount of DltEextra in the test.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS analysis with increased enzyme concentration

claim: No difference with the control sample was observed for LTA incubated with DltES128A catalytic mutant protein or with DacA1.
source: In contrast, no difference with the control sample was observed for LTA incubated with DltES128A catalytic mutant protein or with DacA1 (Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3d and Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: DltE possesses a D-Ala esterase activity that cleaves the ester bond between the substituting D-Ala and Gro in LTA chains.
source: These results establish that DltE possesses a D-Ala esterase activity that cleaves the ester bond between the substituting D-Ala and Gro in LTA chains.
evidence: Based on experimental results showing release of D-Ala from LTA by DltE

claim: DltE is a D-Ala esterase acting on D-Ala-LTA.
source: These structural features are in agreement with the ability of DltE to bind and hydrolyse D-Ala-LTA, and, together with the biochemical data, they confirm that DltE is a D-Ala esterase acting on D-Ala-LTA.
evidence: Based on integration of structural and biochemical data

claim: D-Ala was released in appreciable amounts from LpNC8 (WT) cells upon mild alkaline hydrolysis.
source: As previously observed upon mild alkaline hydrolysis, D-Ala was released in appreciable amounts from LpNC8 (WT) cells14 (Figure 4a), whereas no D-Ala was released from an isogenic mutant deleted for the entire dlt operon (Matos et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a and citation to Matos et al., 2017

claim: No D-Ala was released from an isogenic mutant deleted for the entire dlt operon upon mild alkaline hydrolysis.
source: As previously observed upon mild alkaline hydrolysis, D-Ala was released in appreciable amounts from LpNC8 (WT) cells14 (Figure 4a), whereas no D-Ala was released from an isogenic mutant deleted for the entire dlt operon (Matos et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matos et al., 2017

claim: There was a significant reduction (around 70%) of D-Ala esterified to LTAs in ΔdltE mutant cells.
source: However, we observed a significant reduction (around 70%) of D-Ala esterified to LTAs in ΔdltE mutant cells and an even higher reduction (around 93%) for DltES128A catalytic mutant cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on D-Ala release from mutant cells

claim: There was an even higher reduction (around 93%) of D-Ala esterified to LTAs for DltES128A catalytic mutant cells.
source: However, we observed a significant reduction (around 70%) of D-Ala esterified to LTAs in ΔdltE mutant cells and an even higher reduction (around 93%) for DltES128A catalytic mutant cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on D-Ala release from mutant cells

claim: The esterase activity of DltE, in addition to the activities of DltX, A, B, C, and D, contributes to the D-alanylation machinery of LTAs in bacterial cells.
source: These results indicate that the esterase activity of DltE, in addition to the activities of DltX, A, B, C, and D, contributes to the D-alanylation machinery of LTAs in bacterial cells.
evidence: Based on inference from D-Ala content in mutant strains

claim: Both ΔdltE and dltES128A mutations did not affect the ability of Lp to thrive in the fly niche.
source: Both mutations did not affect the ability of Lp to thrive in the fly niche but significantly altered the ability of Lp to support larval growth and developmental timing (Figure 4b–d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by CFU data shown in Figure 4d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Both ΔdltE and dltES128A mutations significantly altered the ability of Lp to support larval growth and developmental timing.
source: Both mutations did not affect the ability of Lp to thrive in the fly niche but significantly altered the ability of Lp to support larval growth and developmental timing (Figure 4b–d and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by larval size and developmental timing data shown in Figure 4b-c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: DltE activity is required to sustain Drosophila juvenile growth.
source: These results demonstrate that DltE activity is required to sustain Drosophila juvenile growth and together with the structural and biochemical insights on DltE activity point to the importance of D-Ala-LTAs as cues supporting Drosophila growth.
evidence: Based on phenotypic analysis of flies associated with DltE mutants

claim: A similar amount of D-Ala esterified to the cell envelope was measured in ΔtagO mutant cells compared to WT cells.
source: A similar amount of D-Ala esterified to the cell envelope was measured in ΔtagO mutant cells compared to WT cells, whereas a strong reduction of D-Ala (around 72%) was observed in ΔltaS mutant cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by D-Ala quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a

claim: A strong reduction of D-Ala (around 72%) was observed in ΔltaS mutant cells.
source: A similar amount of D-Ala esterified to the cell envelope was measured in ΔtagO mutant cells compared to WT cells, whereas a strong reduction of D-Ala (around 72%) was observed in ΔltaS mutant cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by D-Ala quantification data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a

claim: The absence of LTA chain synthesis in ΔltaS mutant was confirmed by western blot with anti-LTA monoclonal antibody.
source: The absence of LTA chain synthesis in ΔltaS mutant was confirmed by western blot with anti-LTA monoclonal antibody (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b

claim: LTA are D-alanylated but not WTA in LpNC8.
source: These results confirm that LTA are D-alanylated but not WTA as determined above by NMR analysis of purified polymers (Figure 3).
evidence: Based on D-Ala content in ΔtagO and ΔltaS mutants combined with NMR data

claim: WT and ΔtagO strains support optimal Drosophila juvenile growth when associated with germ-free animals.
source: When associated with germ-free animals, WT and ΔtagO strains support optimal Drosophila juvenile growth while Δdltop or ΔltaS strains largely fail to do so despite colonizing well their host's niche (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1c, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by larval size data shown in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a

claim: Δdltop or ΔltaS strains largely fail to support optimal Drosophila juvenile growth despite colonizing well their host's niche.
source: When associated with germ-free animals, WT and ΔtagO strains support optimal Drosophila juvenile growth while Δdltop or ΔltaS strains largely fail to do so despite colonizing well their host's niche (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1c, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by larval size and CFU data shown in Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1c, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a

claim: LTA are important molecules mediating Lp's support to Drosophila juvenile growth.
source: These data demonstrate that LTA are important molecules mediating Lp's support to Drosophila juvenile growth.
evidence: Based on phenotypic analysis of flies associated with ΔltaS mutant

claim: Presence of D-Ala esterified to LTA chains (in WT and ΔtagO strains) correlates well with strains ability to support Drosophila's growth.
source: Accordingly, presence of D-Ala esterified to LTA chains (in WT and ΔtagO strains) correlates well with strains ability to support Drosophila's growth.
evidence: Based on correlation between D-Ala-LTA presence and growth support phenotype

claim: D-Ala-LTA presence is required for Lp-mediated Drosophila juvenile growth promotion phenotype.
source: Indeed, D-Ala-LTA presence is required for Lp-mediated Drosophila juvenile growth promotion phenotype (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a and b, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced growth with strains lacking D-Ala-LTA

claim: In the absence of D-Ala-LTA (in Δdltop) or LTA (in ΔltaS), Drosophila larvae are smaller.
source: In the absence of D-Ala-LTA (in Δdltop) or LTA (in ΔltaS), Drosophila larvae are smaller (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by larval size measurements shown in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a

claim: D-Ala-LTAs from Lp play a key role in supporting Drosophila juvenile growth.
source: Taken collectively these data reinforce the notion that D-Ala-LTAs from Lp play a key role in supporting Drosophila juvenile growth.
evidence: Based on integration of genetic and phenotypic data

claim: Dredd mutant larvae associated with ΔltaS are compromised in their juvenile growth potential.
source: As previously observed upon association with the Δdltop mutant, Dredd mutant larvae associated with ΔltaS are compromised in their juvenile growth potential (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a) and their ability to stimulate intestinal peptidase expression (Jon66Cii and Jon65Ai; Figure 5c and d and Figure 5—figure supplement 2b and c).
evidence: Supported by larval size data shown in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a

claim: Dredd mutant larvae associated with ΔltaS are compromised in their ability to stimulate intestinal peptidase expression (Jon66Cii and Jon65Ai).
source: As previously observed upon association with the Δdltop mutant, Dredd mutant larvae associated with ΔltaS are compromised in their juvenile growth potential (Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a) and their ability to stimulate intestinal peptidase expression (Jon66Cii and Jon65Ai; Figure 5c and d and Figure 5—figure supplement 2b and c).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5c and d and Figure 5—figure supplement 2b and c

claim: Juvenile growth and intestinal peptidase expression were not markedly affected in ΔtagO-associated Dredd larvae.
source: However, juvenile growth and intestinal peptidase expression were not markedly affected in ΔtagO-associated Dredd larvae (Figure 5a–d and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a–c).
evidence: Supported by larval size and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5a-d and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a-c

claim: There is a cumulative effect of not having D-Ala-LTA (Δdltop) or not having LTA at all (ΔltaS) and altering host mDAP-PG sensing.
source: Importantly, we observed a cumulative effect of not having D-Ala-LTA (Δdltop) or not having LTA at all (ΔltaS) and altering host mDAP-PG sensing (compare WT -yw- and Dredd conditions, Figure 5a–d and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a–c).
evidence: Supported by comparison of phenotypes in WT and Dredd backgrounds shown in Figure 5a-d and Figure 5—figure supplement 2a-c

claim: Both mDAP-PG fragments and D-Ala-LTAs signals are required for optimal support to larval growth by Lp.
source: These results therefore support the notion that both signals are required for optimal support to larval growth by Lp and that in addition to mDAP-PG fragments, D-Ala-LTAs are likely an additional cue sensed by Drosophila enterocytes.
evidence: Based on cumulative effects observed in genetic experiments

claim: D-Ala-LTAs are likely an additional cue sensed by Drosophila enterocytes in addition to mDAP-PG fragments.
source: These results therefore support the notion that both signals are required for optimal support to larval growth by Lp and that in addition to mDAP-PG fragments, D-Ala-LTAs are likely an additional cue sensed by Drosophila enterocytes.
evidence: Based on cumulative effects observed in genetic experiments

claim: Daily supplementation with purified WTA or PG either from WT or ΔdltXABCD strains did not impact the growth of GF or Δdltop-associated larvae.
source: Daily supplementation with purified WTA or PG either from WT or ΔdltXABCD strains did not impact the growth of GF or Δdltop-associated larvae (Figure 6b and c and Figure 6—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: Supported by larval size measurements shown in Figure 6b and c and Figure 6—figure supplement 1a and b

claim: Daily supplementation of purified LTA isolated from WT (D-Ala-LTAs) to larvae associated with the Δdltop strain shows a growth-promoting effect that leads to increased larval size.
source: In contrast, the daily supplementation of purified LTA isolated from WT (D-Ala-LTAs) to larvae associated with the Δdltop strain shows a growth-promoting effect that leads to increased larval size in this condition compared to the non-supplemented control (Figure 6d and e).
evidence: Supported by larval size measurements shown in Figure 6d and e

claim: The growth-promoting effect of LTA supplementation was not observed in GF and WT-associated animals nor when Δdltop associated larvae were supplemented with non-alanylated-LTAs isolated from ΔdltXABCD strain.
source: This growth-promoting effect was not observed in GF and WT-associated animals nor when Δdltop associated larvae were supplemented with non-alanylated-LTAs isolated from ΔdltXABCD strain (Figure 6d and e and Figure 6—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: Supported by larval size measurements shown in Figure 6d and e and Figure 6—figure supplement 1c and d

claim: ΔltaS-associated larvae showed improved larval growth upon supplementation with LTA purified from WT (D-Ala-LTAs) but not from LTAs purified from ΔdltXABCD strain (i.e. non-alanylated-LTAs).
source: We repeated the similar experiment with ΔltaS-associated larvae and again observed an improved larval growth upon supplementation with LTA purified from WT (D-Ala-LTAs) but not from LTAs purified from ΔdltXABCD strain (i.e. non-alanylated-LTAs) (Figure 6e and Figure 6—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by larval size measurements shown in Figure 6e and Figure 6—figure supplement 1d

claim: D-Ala-LTAs are necessary and sufficient to restore Drosophila juvenile growth.
source: These results therefore establish that D-Ala-LTAs are necessary and sufficient to restore Drosophila juvenile growth.
evidence: Based on rescue experiments with purified D-Ala-LTAs

claim: Supplementation with D-Ala-LTAs was sufficient to recapitulate the effect of WT strain on intestinal peptidase expression even in the absence of any mDAP-PG signal.
source: We observed that supplementation with D-Ala-LTAs was sufficient to recapitulate the effect of WT strain on intestinal peptidase expression even in the absence of any mDAP-PG signal (Figure 5b, Figure 6f and g, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Dredd mutant background shown in Figure 6f and g and Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: In addition to and independently of mDAP-PG signaling, D-Ala-LTAs are important direct bacterial cues supporting intestinal peptidase expression and Drosophila juvenile growth.
source: Taken collectively, our results demonstrate that in addition to and independently of mDAP-PG signaling, D-Ala-LTAs are important direct bacterial cues supporting intestinal peptidase expression and Drosophila juvenile growth.
evidence: Based on integration of genetic and supplementation experiments

claim: DltE is not a bona fide PBP as it does not bind penicillin nor modifies Lp PG.
source: Here, using complementary structural, biochemical, and genetic approaches, we reveal that the protein encoded by the first gene of this operon (now renamed DltE) is not a bona fide PBP as it does not bind penicillin nor modifies Lp PG.
evidence: Based on penicillin binding assays and PG activity tests

claim: DltE is a D-alanine esterase acting upon LTA.
source: Instead, we establish that DltE is a D-alanine esterase acting upon LTA.
evidence: Based on structural and biochemical characterization

claim: DltE contributes together with the other proteins encoded by the dlt operon (the DltX-A-B-C-D machinery) to the alanylation of LTA on its glycerol residues.
source: While studying its physiological function, we discovered that DltE contributes together with the other proteins encoded by the dlt operon (the DltX-A-B-C-D machinery) to the alanylation of LTA on its glycerol residues.
evidence: Based on D-Ala content analysis in mutant strains

claim: Only LTA and not WTA are alanylated in LpNC8.
source: The study of DltE's substrates gave insights on the structure and composition of LpNC8's TAs, which revealed that only LTA and not WTA are alanylated in this strain.
evidence: Based on NMR analysis of purified TAs

claim: LTAs alanylated by the DltE/X/A/B/C/D complex (but not WTA, which are not alanylated, nor non-alanylated LTA) act as direct bacterial clues supporting Drosophila intestinal function and juvenile growth.
source: Finally, prompted by this strain-specific feature and the importance of the dltEXABCD operon for LpNC8-mediated support to Drosophila growth, we identified that LTAs alanylated by the DltE/X/A/B/C/D complex (but not WTA, which are not alanylated, nor non-alanylated LTA) act as direct bacterial clues supporting Drosophila intestinal function and juvenile growth.
evidence: Based on genetic and supplementation experiments

claim: DltE may be involved in the control of D-Ala distribution on the LTA chains.
source: We posit that DltE may be involved in the control of D-Ala distribution on the LTA chains and DltE inactivation would result in impaired functioning of the whole D-alanylation machinery.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the discrepancy between enzymatic activity and mutant phenotype

claim: DltE inactivation would result in impaired functioning of the whole D-alanylation machinery.
source: We posit that DltE may be involved in the control of D-Ala distribution on the LTA chains and DltE inactivation would result in impaired functioning of the whole D-alanylation machinery.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the discrepancy between enzymatic activity and mutant phenotype

claim: The ability to produce poly-(Gro-phosphate) WTA chains is a strain-specific feature in Lp as the tag gene cluster is only found in 22 out of 54 strains recently studied at the genomic level.
source: The ability to produce poly-(Gro-phosphate) WTA chains is a strain-specific feature in Lp as the tag gene cluster is only found in 22 out of 54 strains recently studied at the genomic level (Martino et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martino et al., 2016

claim: In the case of the LpWCFS1 strain, despite its genome carrying the genetic information to synthetize both types of WTA (poly-(Gro-phosphate) and poly-(Rbo-phosphate)), only poly(Gro-phosphate) WTAs were detected at steady state.
source: However, in the case of the LpWCFS1 strain, despite its genome carrying the genetic information to synthetize both types of WTA (poly-(Gro-phosphate) and poly-(Rbo-phosphate)), only poly(Gro-phosphate) WTAs were detected at steady state (Bron et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bron et al., 2012

claim: In other L. plantarum strains such as LpWCFS1, WTA appears to be D-alanylated.
source: This is an original feature as in other L. plantarum strains such as LpWCFS1, WTA appears to be D-alanylated (Bron et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bron et al., 2012

claim: The Drosophila midgut is lined with both thick chitinous matrix and thin mucus layer, yet permeable to large macromolecules and small nutrient particles.
source: Given that L. plantarum is a gut luminal microbe and that the Drosophila midgut is lined with both thick chitinous matrix and thin mucus layer, yet permeable to large macromolecules and small nutrient particles (Lemaitre and Miguel-Aliaga, 2013), how exactly these macromolecules associated to the bacterial cell membrane reach the enterocytes remains elusive.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lemaitre and Miguel-Aliaga, 2013

claim: LTA chains may be shed after cleavage of the lipid anchor.
source: Similarly to PG fragments, which are shaded in the extracellular media during bacterial cell division, LTA chains may also be shed after cleavage of the lipid anchor (Neuhaus and Baddiley, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Neuhaus and Baddiley, 2003

claim: LpNC8 has the ability to release microvesicles of multi-nanometers ranges.
source: In addition, our recent findings report LpNC8's ability to release microvesicles of multi-nanometers ranges (Grenier et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Grenier et al., 2021

claim: Other Lactobacillus strains form microvesicles containing LTAs that are endocytosed by mammalian enterocytes.
source: This observation is coupled to previous reports showing that other Lactobacillus strains form microvesicles containing LTAs that are endocytosed by mammalian enterocytes (Champagne-Jorgensen et al., 2021), it is tempting to speculate that LpNC8 D-Ala-LTAs are released via bacterial microvesicles cargo.
evidence: Supported by citation to Champagne-Jorgensen et al., 2021

claim: It is tempting to speculate that LpNC8 D-Ala-LTAs are released via bacterial microvesicles cargo.
source: This observation is coupled to previous reports showing that other Lactobacillus strains form microvesicles containing LTAs that are endocytosed by mammalian enterocytes (Champagne-Jorgensen et al., 2021), it is tempting to speculate that LpNC8 D-Ala-LTAs are released via bacterial microvesicles cargo.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on observations in other systems

claim: The Drosophila host would capitalize on microvesicle release by endocytosing cleaved LTA or such cargo and sense these bacterial cues through pattern recognition receptors expressed in enterocytes.
source: The Drosophila host would capitalize on these features by endocytosing cleaved LTA or such cargo and sense these bacterial cues through pattern recognition receptors expressed in enterocytes.
evidence: Speculative model for how D-Ala-LTAs reach and are sensed by enterocytes

claim: PG fragments are sensed intracellularly in the Drosophila midgut by PGRP-LE, which signals the Imd pathway to stimulate intestinal peptidase expression.
source: PG fragments are sensed intracellularly in the Drosophila midgut by PGRP-LE, which signals the Imd pathway to stimulate intestinal peptidase expression.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from previous research

claim: Another signaling cascade beyond the one engaged by PGRP-LE is leading to D-Ala-LTA-mediated intestinal peptidase induction.
source: How D-Ala-LTAs are sensed and signal in enterocytes remain elusive, but our results support the notion that another signaling cascade beyond the one engaged by PGRP-LE is leading to D-Ala-LTA-mediated intestinal peptidase induction.
evidence: Based on observations in Dredd mutant background

claim: Drosophila ensures an optimal intestinal response to bacterial cues by using additive rather than interdependent signals converging locally to intestinal peptidase expression and macroscopically to enhanced juvenile growth.
source: Taken together, it seems that Drosophila ensures an optimal intestinal response to bacterial cues by using additive rather than interdependent signals converging locally to intestinal peptidase expression and macroscopically to enhanced juvenile growth.
evidence: Based on cumulative effects observed in genetic experiments

claim: There are strong analogies of the impact of L. plantarum strains on Drosophila and mouse growth.
source: Given the strong analogies of the impact of L. plantarum strains on Drosophila and mouse growth (Schwarzer et al., 2016) and previous work focusing on LTA in host-Gram-positive bacteria interactions (Champagne-Jorgensen et al., 2021; Hara et al., 2018), an exciting perspective will be to test the contribution of D-Ala-LTA to L. plantarum-mediated host growth promotion in other symbiotic models including mammals.
evidence: Supported by citations to Schwarzer et al., 2016, Champagne-Jorgensen et al., 2021, and Hara et al., 2018

claim: An exciting perspective will be to test the contribution of D-Ala-LTA to L. plantarum-mediated host growth promotion in other symbiotic models including mammals.
source: Given the strong analogies of the impact of L. plantarum strains on Drosophila and mouse growth (Schwarzer et al., 2016) and previous work focusing on LTA in host-Gram-positive bacteria interactions (Champagne-Jorgensen et al., 2021; Hara et al., 2018), an exciting perspective will be to test the contribution of D-Ala-LTA to L. plantarum-mediated host growth promotion in other symbiotic models including mammals.
evidence: Authors' perspective on future research directions

claim: The extracellular domain of DltE (DltEextra 34–397) is not able to bind penicillin.
source: Supporting this, we showed that the extracellular catalytic domain of DltE (DltEextra 34–397) is not able to bind penicillin although this property is a hallmark of serine type D-alanyl-D-alanine carboxypeptidases that belongs to the PBP (penicillin binding proteins) protein family (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by MST data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2

claim: The ability to bind penicillin is a hallmark of serine type D-alanyl-D-alanine carboxypeptidases that belongs to the PBP (penicillin binding proteins) protein family.
source: Supporting this, we showed that the extracellular catalytic domain of DltE (DltEextra 34–397) is not able to bind penicillin although this property is a hallmark of serine type D-alanyl-D-alanine carboxypeptidases that belongs to the PBP (penicillin binding proteins) protein family (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of PBP protein family

claim: The extracellular domain of DltE consists of two subdomains: an α-β sandwich (residues 76–126 and 246–397) and an α-helix-rich region (residues 127–245).
source: The domain consists of two subdomains, an α-β sandwich (residues 76–126 and 246–397) that form a five strand (β1–β5) antiparallel β-sheet flanked by 5 α-helices (α2, α9–α12) and an α-helix-rich region (residues 127–245) folding in 6 α-helices (α3-α8) (Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by X-ray crystallography structure shown in Figure 1a and Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: DDCP from Streptomyces exhibits the classical β-lactamase fold of PBPs.
source: DltE is structurally homologous to the D-Ala-D-Ala carboxypeptidase R61 (DDCP) from Streptomyces (Figure 1b and c; Kelly et al., 1986; McDonough et al., 2002) that exhibits the classical β-lactamase fold of PBPs (Figure 1b).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison and citations to Kelly et al., 1986 and McDonough et al., 2002

claim: The catalytic Tyr213 from the second motif is conserved in DltE and expected to function as a general base during the acylation step.
source: The positions of the active site S-X-X-K motif (128SIQK131), containing the catalytic Ser128 and Lys131 residues, and the catalytic Tyr213 from the second motif are conserved (Figure 1a and b and Figure 2). These last two residues are expected to function as a general base during the acylation step and function as a relay mechanism for the transfer of a proton from the incoming substrate to the departing catalytic serine.
evidence: Based on structural analysis and comparison with known enzyme mechanisms

claim: Ser128 and Lys131 are expected to function as a relay mechanism for the transfer of a proton from the incoming substrate to the departing catalytic serine.
source: The positions of the active site S-X-X-K motif (128SIQK131), containing the catalytic Ser128 and Lys131 residues, and the catalytic Tyr213 from the second motif are conserved (Figure 1a and b and Figure 2). These last two residues are expected to function as a general base during the acylation step and function as a relay mechanism for the transfer of a proton from the incoming substrate to the departing catalytic serine.
evidence: Based on structural analysis and comparison with known enzyme mechanisms

claim: DltE contains an extra α-helix (α1) at the N-terminus of the catalytic domain.
source: Second, DltE contains an extra α-helix (α1) at the N-terminus of the catalytic domain (Figure 1c), as well as three major structural differences affecting the regions lining the sides of the active site of DDCP and responsible for its cavity-like shape (Figure 1c, e and g)
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1c

claim: The loop between α8 and α9 (residues 257–283 in DltE) connecting the two subdomains is slightly shorter in DltE and adopts a different position compared to DDCP.
source: and (3) the loop between α8 and α9 (residues 257–283 in DltE) connecting the two subdomains is slightly shorter in DltE and adopts a different position (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 1c

claim: The loop between α8 and α9 was described as the Ω-like loop in β-lactamases and PBP proteins and shown to play a key role in the maintenance of the active site topology and in the enzymatic activity.
source: This last difference is of particular interest because this loop was described as the Ω-like loop in β-lactamases and PBP proteins (Fetrow, 1995; Yi et al., 2016) and shown to play a key role in the maintenance of the active site topology and in the enzymatic activity (Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fetrow, 1995 and Yi et al., 2016

claim: Tartrate and TCEP molecules are anchored by an interaction network that involves eight different residues, among which are the conserved active site nucleophile Ser128 and the base Tyr213.
source: Intriguingly, these two molecules are anchored by an interaction network that involves eight different residues, among which are the conserved active site nucleophile Ser128 and the base Tyr213 (Ser 62 and Tyr 159 in DDCP; Figure 2a, b and e).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2a, b and e

claim: The catalytic Ser128 with the hydroxyl group of its side chain positioned at only 2.7 Å away from a carboxylic group of TCEP and tartrate is ideally placed as it would activate a substrate for the enzyme acylation event.
source: Importantly, the catalytic Ser128 with the hydroxyl group of its side chain positioned at only 2.7 Å away from a carboxylic group of TCEP and tartrate is ideally placed as it would activate a substrate for the enzyme acylation event as described for DDCP (McDonough et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis and citation to McDonough et al., 2002

claim: The tartrate and TCEP molecule may mimic the nature and position of the natural substrate of DltE in its active site.
source: This suggests that the tartrate and TCEP molecule may mimic the nature and position of the natural substrate of DltE in its active site and that the acylation/deacylation step of the catalytic reaction is probably preserved in DltE (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: Based on inference from structural analysis

claim: The acylation/deacylation step of the catalytic reaction is probably preserved in DltE.
source: This suggests that the tartrate and TCEP molecule may mimic the nature and position of the natural substrate of DltE in its active site and that the acylation/deacylation step of the catalytic reaction is probably preserved in DltE (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: Based on inference from structural analysis

claim: A Tyr residue (Tyr338 in DltE) interacting with TCEP or tartrate replaces the conserved arginine (Arg285 in DDCP) in carboxypeptidases.
source: Notably, a Tyr residue (Tyr338 in DltE) interacting with TCEP or tartrate replaces the conserved arginine (Arg285 in DDCP) in carboxypeptidases.
evidence: Supported by structural comparison

claim: The conserved arginine (Arg285 in DDCP) is key for the recognition of the terminal carboxylate of the peptide substrate and the carboxypeptidase activity.
source: This arginine is key for the recognition of the terminal carboxylate of the peptide substrate and the carboxypeptidase activity (McDonough et al., 2002; Figure 2b, d and e).
evidence: Supported by citation to McDonough et al., 2002 and structural comparison

claim: The interactions involving motif 2 and 3 that stabilizes the substrate in DDCP and in particular the penultimate D-Ala residue of the peptide substrate are largely altered in DltE.
source: Furthermore, the interactions involving motif 2 and 3 that stabilizes the substrate in DDCP and in particular the penultimate D-Ala residue of the peptide substrate are also largely altered (Figure 2b, d and e).
evidence: Supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 2b, d and e

claim: In DltE, residues specific to DltE (Tyr338, His347, Arg345, and Leu349) stabilize the TCEP or tartrate molecules.
source: Instead, residues specific to DltE (Tyr338, His347, Arg345, and Leu349) stabilize the TCEP or tartrate molecules (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: Supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 2a and b

claim: DltE would not be able to recognize the D-Ala-D-Ala terminal end of a stem peptide as DDCP does.
source: Taken collectively, our structural data suggest that DltE would not be able to recognize the D-Ala-D-Ala terminal end of a stem peptide as DDCP does and that DltE would not be a DD-carboxypeptidase.
evidence: Based on inference from structural differences with DDCP

claim: DltE would not be a DD-carboxypeptidase.
source: Taken collectively, our structural data suggest that DltE would not be able to recognize the D-Ala-D-Ala terminal end of a stem peptide as DDCP does and that DltE would not be a DD-carboxypeptidase.
evidence: Based on inference from structural differences with DDCP

claim: In L. plantarum PG precursors, a D-Lac residue rather than the more common D-Ala is present in position 5 of the peptide stem with an ester bond between D-Ala4 and D-Lac5.
source: In L. plantarum PG precursors, a D-Lac residue rather than the more common D-Ala is present in position 5 of the peptide stem with an ester bond between D-Ala4 and D-Lac5 (Ferain et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferain et al., 1996

claim: DacA1 and/or DacA2 could behave as carboxylesterases removing the terminal D-Lac from PG.
source: As D-Lac residues are not detected in WT strain (Bernard et al., 2011), this indicates that DacA1 and/or DacA2 could behave as carboxylesterases removing the terminal D-Lac.
evidence: Based on detection of disaccharide-depsipentapeptide in ΔdacA1A2 mutant and citation to Bernard et al., 2011

claim: D-Lac residues are not detected in WT L. plantarum strain.
source: As D-Lac residues are not detected in WT strain (Bernard et al., 2011), this indicates that DacA1 and/or DacA2 could behave as carboxylesterases removing the terminal D-Lac.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bernard et al., 2011

claim: Disaccharide-depsipentapeptide (GlcNAc-MurNAc-L-Ala-D-Gln-mDAP-D-Ala-D-Lac) was detected in LpNC8 ∆dacA1∆dacA2 mutant.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a, we detected the presence of disaccharide-depsipentapeptide (GlcNAc-MurNAc-L-Ala-D-Gln-mDAP-D-Ala-D-Lac).
evidence: Supported by UHPLC analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2a
